<<The Weight of a Century>>

The dressing room was thick with the kind of silence that hums, the sort that settles over a cricketer when the day’s play ends not with defeat, but with the gnawing promise of something greater. Gus Atkinson sat on the bench, his gloves still damp with sweat, his bat propped against the wall like a silent witness to the chaos he had just tamed. Around him, teammates murmured in low tones, their voices a distant murmur beneath the roar of his own thoughts. Seventy-four not out. A first-class century within reach. The numbers should have been a triumph, but instead, they coiled around his ribs, tightening with every passing second. Outside, the London sky darkened, and with it, the weight of expectation pressed down like a second skin.

Sleep came in fragments—jagged, restless. Atkinson tossed beneath the thin hotel sheets, his mind replaying the day’s strokes in an endless loop. The way the ball had kissed the edge of his bat, the way Root’s steady presence had anchored him when the innings threatened to unravel. He imagined the morning: the walk back to the crease, the eyes of the crowd, the Sri Lankan bowlers circling like sharks. Would his hands tremble? Would the ball suddenly seem smaller, heavier, impossible to hit? The fear was a living thing, slithering through his veins, whispering that the night was too long, the stakes too high. But when dawn broke, he rose before the alarm, his body moving on instinct, as if the hours of dread had been someone else’s burden.

The first ball of the day was a gift—a gentle full toss from Lahiru Kumara, drifting down the leg side. Atkinson didn’t think. He swung, and the ball raced away for four, the sound of leather on willow cracking through the tension like a gunshot. The next delivery was different, a seaming ball outside off, but his cover drive was flawless, the bat meeting the ball with the precision of a metronome. The crowd erupted, but Atkinson barely heard them. His focus was a tunnel, narrow and unyielding, blocking out the noise, the pressure, the ghosts of the night before. He was in the zone now, and nothing—not the lbw decision that nearly cost him, not the inside edge that shaved his stumps—could shake him.

Chain reactions are funny like that. One boundary begets another, confidence snowballing until the impossible feels inevitable. Sri Lanka’s bowlers, so menacing the day before, now looked like schoolboys lost in a storm. Kumara, the man who had nearly sent Atkinson packing, was suddenly the architect of his triumph. A pull shot, executed with such disdain that it might as well have been a middle finger to doubt, sent the ball rocketing to the boundary. The England balcony erupted in air punches, but Atkinson’s face remained a mask of quiet intensity. He had spent the night wrestling with demons; now, he was exorcising them, one stroke at a time.

When the century came, it was almost anticlimactic. A drive past mid-off, the ball skimming the outfield grass like a stone across water, and then the numbers on the scoreboard flickered to 103. Atkinson raised his bat, not in wild celebration, but in quiet acknowledgment—a nod to the hours of torment, the sleepless night, the voice in his head that had screamed *what if?* The Lord’s crowd roared, but for Atkinson, the real victory was the silence that followed. The silence of a mind finally at peace, of a man who had stared into the abyss and refused to blink. As he walked off the field, the weight of the century was still there, but now it felt different. Lighter. Like a trophy he had earned not just with his bat, but with his will.
